Imagine trying to build a chat application where you constantly have to ask the server, 'Has anyone sent a new message?' This is inefficient and creates a poor user experience. Understanding and utilizing this event system is key to building dynamic, responsive, and truly interactive decentralized applications that feel alive and connected to the chain's real-time pulse. It shifts your dApp from a passive observer to an active participant in the blockchain's ongoing narrative. content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Subscribe to New Block Headers
Real-time Monitoring

Subscribing to New Block Headers

Monitoring basic chain activity with subscribeNewHeads

The `subscribeNewHeads` Method

This Polkadot-JS API method provides a stream of new block headers as they are produced, offering a basic, real-time view of chain activity.

Crucial `unsub()` Function

The subscription returns an unsub() function. Calling this is vital to terminate the subscription and prevent resource leaks when updates are no longer needed.

Key Takeaway

api.rpc.chain.subscribeNewHeads() is your entry point for real-time chain monitoring, but always remember to call unsub().

// subscribeBlocks.js
const { ApiPromise, WsProvider } = require('@polkadot/api');

async function main () {
  const provider = new WsProvider('ws://127.0.0.1:9944');
  const api = await ApiPromise.create({ provider });

  console.log('Subscribing to new block headers...');

  // Subscribe to new headers
  const unsub = await api.rpc.chain.subscribeNewHeads((header) => {
    console.log(`Chain is at block #${header.number}: ${header.hash.toHex()}`);
  });

  // Keep the connection open for 60 seconds, then unsubscribe
  setTimeout(() => {
    unsub();
    console.log('Unsubscribed from new block headers.');
    api.disconnect();
  }, 60000); // Unsubscribe after 1 minute
}

main().catch(console.error);
Terminal Output
Subscribing to new block headers...
Chain is at block #12345: 0x...
Chain is at block #12346: 0x...
...
Unsubscribed from new block headers.

screens.title: Managing Subscriptions with `unsub()`
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding and properly utilizing the unsub open parenthesis close parenthesis function is not just good practice; it's critical for the health and efficiency of your dApps. When you initiate a subscription, you're essentially opening a persistent connection to your Substrate node, asking it to continuously send you updates. If you don't explicitly close this connection when it's no longer needed, it remains open, consuming network resources and potentially leading to memory leaks in long-running applications. Imagine a web application where users navigate between different pages. If each page subscribes to events but never unsubscribes, you could end up with dozens or even hundreds of active, unnecessary connections, bogging down both the client and the node. The unsub open parenthesis close parenthesis function provides a clean and controlled way to terminate these subscriptions, ensuring that resources are freed up and your application remains performant. It's a simple call, but its impact on application stability and resource management is profound. Always consider the lifecycle of your subscriptions and integrate unsub open parenthesis close parenthesis into your cleanup routines, whether it's on component unmount in a UI framework or at the end of a script's execution.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Managing Subscriptions
Best Practices

Managing Subscriptions with unsub()

Preventing resource leaks and ensuring efficient dApp operation

Why `unsub()` is Crucial

Subscriptions create persistent connections. Without unsub(), these connections remain open, consuming network bandwidth and node resources unnecessarily.

Preventing Memory Leaks

In long-running applications or single-page applications, unmanaged subscriptions can lead to memory leaks, degrading performance over time.

Integration into Lifecycle

Always integrate unsub() into your application's cleanup logic, such as component unmounts in UI frameworks or script termination.

Key Takeaway

Always call the unsub() function returned by subscription methods to ensure proper resource management and application stability.

Unmanaged Subscriptions
Continuous Network Traffic
Memory Leaks
Degraded Performance
Clean & Efficient!

Event Stream

Subscribing to All System Events

Listening for all on-chain activity with api.query.system.events()

Beyond Block Headers

While block headers confirm chain progress, system events provide granular details about what actually occurred within those blocks, such as transactions and state changes.

The `api.query.system.events()` Method

This powerful Polkadot-JS API method allows you to subscribe to a stream of all events emitted by the Substrate runtime and its pallets in newly finalized blocks.

api.query.system.events() is essential for building dApps that need to react to specific, detailed changes on the blockchain, not just new blocks.

Received ${events.length} events in new block:`);

Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Decoding Event Data
Event Structure

Decoding Event Data

Understanding event.section, event.method, and event.data

event.section: The Origin

Identifies the Substrate pallet or module that emitted the event (e.g., balances, system, templateModule).

event.method: The Action

Specifies the particular type of event within its section (e.g., Transfer, ExtrinsicSuccess, SomethingStored).

event.data: The Parameters

An array containing the specific arguments or values emitted by the event. Requires knowledge of expected order and types for correct decoding.

Key Takeaway

Properly decoding event.section, event.method, and event.data is crucial for extracting meaningful information from blockchain events.

Event Decoding Flow
1
Receive EventRecord
2
Extract event & phase
3
Identify event.section & event.method
4
Parse event.data (e.g., toHuman())
5
React to Decoded Event

screens.title: Filtering for Specific Events: `balances.Transfer`
screens.narratorSegment: Once you're subscribed to the general stream of system events, the next crucial step is to filter for the specific events that matter to your application. Imagine a busy city with many different types of vehicles; you're only interested in the delivery trucks. In Substrate, this means looking for a particular event. section and event. method combination. A very common and practical example is filtering for a balances. Transfer event. This event is emitted whenever tokens are moved between accounts. By checking if event. section is 'balances' and event. method is 'Transfer', you can isolate these specific events from the broader stream. Once identified, you can then access the event. data array, which for a transfer event typically contains the from account, the to account, and the amount transferred. Using methods like to Human open parenthesis close parenthesis helps convert these raw data types into easily understandable strings. This targeted filtering is what allows your dApp to implement precise logic, such as updating a user's balance display, triggering a notification, or initiating a follow-up action, only when a relevant transfer occurs. It transforms a noisy stream of all events into a focused, actionable data feed for your application.

content.html:
Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Filtering Events
Event Filtering

Filtering for Specific Events: balances.Transfer

Targeting relevant events for dApp logic

Why Filter Events?

The chain emits many events. Filtering allows your dApp to focus only on the events relevant to its specific functionality, improving efficiency and clarity.

Identifying `balances.Transfer`

A common use case is detecting token transfers. This is achieved by checking if event.section === 'balances' and event.method === 'Transfer'.

Key Takeaway

Filtering events by their section and method is fundamental for building dApps that react intelligently to specific on-chain actions.

// subscribeEvents.js (filtering excerpt)
const { ApiPromise, WsProvider } = require('@polkadot/api');

async function main () {
  // ... API connection ...

  const unsub = await api.query.system.events((events) => {
    events.forEach((record) => {
      const { event, phase } = record;

      // Check if it's a Balances.Transfer event
      if (event.section === 'balances' && event.method === 'Transfer') {
        const [from, to, amount] = event.data;
        console.log(`    >> TRANSFER: ${from.toHuman()} transferred ${amount.toHuman()} to ${to.toHuman()}`);
      }
    });
  });

  // ... setTimeout for unsubscribing ...
}

main().catch(console.error);

  balances.Transfer:: (phase=ApplyExtrinsic)
    from: 5Grwva...
    to: 5FHZ...
    amount: 1000000000000
    >> TRANSFER: 5Grwva... transferred 1 UNIT to 5FHZ...

screens.title: Filtering for Custom Pallet Events
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond the standard system events, the true extensibility of Substrate shines when you can react to events emitted by your own custom pallets. This is where your dApp can become truly specialized, responding to unique logic and state changes defined within your blockchain. Module 5›Chapter 5.4›Custom Pallet Events
Custom Pallet Integration

Filtering for Custom Pallet Events

Reacting to events from your own Substrate modules

Extending Event-Driven Logic

Your custom pallets can emit unique events. Filtering for these allows your dApp to react to specific, custom logic and state changes defined in your runtime.

Matching `section` and `method`

Similar to system events, you'll filter by matching event.section (your pallet name, e.g., 'templateModule') and event.method (your event name, e.g., 'SomethingStored').

Key Takeaway

Reacting to custom pallet events is crucial for building dApps that are deeply integrated and responsive to your unique blockchain's functionality.

// subscribeEvents.js (custom event filtering)
const { ApiPromise, WsProvider } = require('@polkadot/api');

async function main () {
  // ... API connection and general event subscription ...

  const unsub = await api.query.system.events((events) => {
    events.forEach((record) => {
      const { event, phase } = record;

      // Check for your custom pallet's event (e.g., TemplateModule.SomethingStored)
      if (event.section === 'templateModule' && event.method === 'SomethingStored') {
        const [somethingValue, who] = event.data;
        console.log(`    >> CUSTOM EVENT: SomethingStored: value=${somethingValue.toNumber()} by=${who.toHuman()}`);
      }
    });
  });

  // ... setTimeout for unsubscribing ...
}

main().catch(console.error);

screens.title: Common Mistakes with Custom Runtime APIs
screens.narratorSegment: When working with custom runtime APIs, one of the most frequent pitfalls developers encounter is the 'method not found' error. This typically doesn't mean your code is wrong, but rather that the runtime A P I you're trying to call isn't properly exposed or recognized by your Substrate node. The Substrate framework requires a specific setup to make custom runtime APIs accessible. First, the A P I must be correctly defined within your runtime's src slash lib. rs and runtime slash src slash lib. rs files. This involves implementing the impl underscore runtime underscore apis! macro and defining the A P I's interface. Second, and equally important, this custom A P I must be explicitly exposed in your node's chain underscore spec. rs file. This file dictates the configuration and capabilities of your blockchain, including which runtime APIs are available for external calls. Failing to complete either of these steps will result in the runtime method being unavailable, leading to the dreaded 'method not found' error. Always double-check these configuration files when you encounter such issues. Proper exposure ensures that your dApp can seamlessly interact with the specialized logic you've built into your custom runtime, making your development process much smoother and more predictable.
